newsitem.title: USA: Dow storms to higher close on soothed rate fears.
newsitem.headline: Dow storms to higher close on soothed rate fears.

text.p: U.S. blue chips roared to their biggest point gain in a month as investors grew more confident that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates modestly, if at all, later this month.

Analysts said investors took a second look at Friday's jobs report and traced some strength to seasonal factors. "There's some renewed investor confidence for the time being that inflation and interest rates are not a problem," said Oppenheimer's chief investment strategist Michael Metz.
The Dow rose 74 points, or 1.31 percent, to about 5734.
It was the largest point rise since a 85-point rally on August 2 and put the blue-chip index within a stone's throw of its record-high 5778.00 set on May 22.
The Dow on Friday surged 53 points after a report that August non-farm payrolls rose by 250,000, which was higher than expected though not by as much as many had feared.
"A lot of the new employees were teachers and managerial types. The more you look at it, there's a seasonal swing," said Robert Stovall, president of Stovall/21st Advisers.
"Portfolio managers drew a little courage from the figures and there's the expectation of no move by the Fed," Metz said.
Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management, expects a 25-basis-point tightening at the Fed's next policy-setting meeting on September 24.
"We took the economic smoking gun out of Chairman (Alan) Greenspan's hands, such that a 50-basis-point tightening on September 24 is no longer in the cards," he said.

Still, buying on Monday was focused on blue chips and activity was tepid, analysts said. Gainers beat losers 15-8 on NYSE volume of about 309 million shares, near the sluggish pace of the dog days of August. The Nasdaq Composite rose 0.82 percent to about 1149. The S&P 500 surged 1.23 percent to 664.
"Buying was really concentrated in blue chips. People did not have the courage to trade down," Metz said.
Gold mining stocks fell as inflation fears ebbed, with Comex December gold off $1.60 at $387.20 an ounce. Newmont Gold Co lost 1-3/4 to 52-1/2, and Newmont Mining Corp fell 1-1/8 to 51-3/4.

Stovall said oil stocks, which have been supported by U.S.-Iraq tensions, "have quieted down." Among the Dow components, Chevron rose 1/8 to 60-3/8, Texaco added 1/2 to 93-1/2 and Exxon inched up 1/4 to 84-1/4.
Stovall also said "business-cycle stocks are bouncing."

He noted strength in United Technologies Corp, up 3-1/2 to 115-3/4, International Business Machines Corp, up 2-3/8 to 117-5/8, Caterpillar Inc, up 1-3/4 to 73-1/2, DuPont Co, up one to 84-5/8, and Union Carbide Corp, up 1-7/8 to 45-1/8.
Among individual shares, Lucent Technologies Inc added 1-7/8 to 39. CS First Boston named Lucent its "focus stock of the week."
SGS-Thomson Microelectronics surged four to 43-7/8 in U.S. trading after news that it developed an integrated circuit that protects digital video systems from copyright pirating.

A spate of merger announcements galvanized some buying interest. Big B Inc climbed 3-1/4 to 15-7/8 and was the most active Nasdaq issue after receiving an unsolicited $15-a-share offer from Revco, which slipped 1/8 to 25-1/2.

Britain's Danka Business Systems Plc agreed to buy Eastman Kodak Co's office imaging business and facilities management business for $684 million in cash. Danka surged 6-5/8 to 36-1/2 in U.S. trading, and Kodak slipped 1/2 to 71-3/4.
Also, Phar-Mor Inc and ShopKo Stores Inc said they would merge, creating a new company called Cabot Noble Inc. Phar-Mor lost 3/4 to 7-3/8, and ShopKo lost 1/8 to 16-1/8.
DAKA International slumped 5-3/8 to 10 and DII Group Inc lost four to 19 after warning of earnings shortfalls.

West Coast-based HMOs gained after news of a solid rise in key Medicare payment rates, while some of their East Coast counterparts lagged. The US Health Care Finance Administration said Medicare payment rates to HMOs would rise an average 5.9 percent next year, compared with a 10.1 percent rise in 1996.

The rates are set for each U.S. county, and key counties in California were given rate increases between five and eight percent, while the New York City area was granted a rise of zero to two percent, industry analysts said.

Cypress, Calif.-based PacifiCare Health Systems Inc said it won an overall increase of 6.1 percent for its Medicare plan, while Las Vegas-based Sierra Health Services said its increases included a 6.0 percent rise in southern Nevada and about 8.0 percent in the Houston area. PacifiCare's A shares rose 2-1/4 to 80, and Sierra rose 1-1/8 to 32-1/4.
Oxford Health Plans, with a large portion of its business in the New York City area, was off 1-1/2 to 41-1/2.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 9.32 to 1148.71.
The S&P 500 index rose 8.09 to 663.77.
(Figures official as of 1645 EDT/2045 GMT)
-- Wall Street desk, 212 859 1721
